title: Harvest Festival

jokes.text: Leslie's grandiose buildup to Little Sebastian — 'the best thing to potentially ever happen to anyone anywhere in the history of the Universe' — followed by the reveal of a tiny mini horse.
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers an epic, universe-spanning hyperbolic buildup suggesting something world-shaking is about to be revealed.
jokes.punchline: It's a small horse. The absurd gap between the setup's scale and the mundane reveal is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels simultaneously: it's a perfect misdirection with a hyperbolic setup, it's deeply character-specific (Leslie's unbridled enthusiasm is her defining trait), and the payoff relies entirely on the audience's rational perspective vs. Pawnee's irrational one. The structure is clean and the gap between expectation and reality is maximally funny. Scores 8+ because it also plants the episode's central comedic premise (Li'l Sebastian's inexplicable celebrity) while being funny on its own terms.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everyone, I have a surprise for you!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been planning this for weeks. It's going to change your lives. It's unprecedented. It's extraordinary. It's the most amazing thing that's ever happened to this department.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I present to you... a mini horse!

jokes.text: The entire office erupts in disbelief and joy at seeing Li'l Sebastian while Ben watches, confused.
jokes.setup: Li'l Sebastian is revealed and everyone goes wild — 'I never thought I'd get to meet him!' 'It's really him!'
jokes.punchline: Ben stands apart, utterly baffled, asking 'So what am I missing? What's the deal with the pony?'
jokes.explanation: Ben serves as the audience's surrogate rationalist — his confusion mirrors exactly what any sane viewer feels. The contrast between the unanimous, sincere joy of everyone else and Ben's outsider bewilderment is perfect. Works as character comedy because Ben's role as an outside auditor/rational outsider is being applied to Pawnee's absurd culture. High craft because the comedy is structural and character-driven, not just a random joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Little Sebastian wasn't just a pony. He was a symbol of Pawnee's spirit, our hope, our dreams. And fun fact: Sebastian was also the number one girl's name in Pawnee that year.

jokes.text: 'He's not a pony, man. He's a mini horse. There's a big difference.'
jokes.setup: Ben calls Li'l Sebastian 'the pony,' confused by the fervor.
jokes.punchline: Tom corrects him with complete seriousness, as if this distinction matters enormously in context.
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and perfectly delivered — the joke works because Tom is extremely concerned about the wrong thing. The absurdity is that this is the detail Tom chooses to correct when there are bigger confusions at play. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't understand. It's a tiny horse. Why is everyone so obsessed with a tiny horse?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you don't understand. Little Sebastian isn't just a horse. He's a symbol of hope and joy for this entire community.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's literally just a small pony that eats and poops. I've seen him do both of those things.

jokes.text: 'Son, this horse has an honorary degree from Notre Dame.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks what Li'l Sebastian actually does to explain the fame.
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers this as though it settles the matter completely — an honorary degree from Notre Dame, for a horse.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. It does everything right: it's delivered by Ron, whose stoic authority makes absurdist pronouncements land with maximum weight; the detail is specific and bizarre (Notre Dame, specifically); it treats the absurdity as completely self-evident; and it answers Ben's rational question with a completely irrational non-answer delivered as though it's sufficient. The economy is near-perfect — seven words that do enormous comedic work. The character integration is exceptional: Ron's deadpan certainty is the entire joke. Justifiably an 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. He's not a pony. He's a miniature horse. There's a big difference.

jokes.text: Jerry reveals he and Li'l Sebastian are on the same diabetes medication and calls him his 'Glucotrol buddy.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains that Jerry will be looking after Li'l Sebastian since he's 25 with cataracts and arthritis.
jokes.punchline: Jerry enthusiastically reveals they share a diabetes medication, cooing at the horse like a baby.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed reveal that simultaneously establishes Jerry's haplessness (sharing medication with a horse), his total lack of self-awareness (he's delighted by this), and sets up his later failure to watch the horse. 'Glucotrol buddy' is specific, memorable, and deeply character-specific. Scores 8+ because the joke layers character comedy with absurdism in a way that only Parks and Recreation could write — it's warm, bizarre, and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He's a miniature horse of unparalleled grace and beauty. He has the heart of a champion and the brain of a... slightly above-average horse.

jokes.text: 'Get out.' — Leslie's immediate, flat response to Ben saying he doesn't know what the big deal is about Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.setup: Ben confesses he genuinely doesn't understand the excitement about Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's instant, no-hesitation 'Get out.' — treating this as a fireable or banishable offense.
jokes.explanation: Two words, maximum impact. The joke is structurally perfect: the absurdity of treating Li'l Sebastian skepticism as an offense worthy of expulsion, delivered without a beat of hesitation. Leslie's character integration is perfect — she's incapable of accepting that someone could not share her enthusiasms. The economy score is as high as it gets. Scores 8+ because the brevity and character specificity make it one of the most quotable moments in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Hey there, little guy. You know, I have a lot of back problems too. Maybe we can bond over that.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I also have a really weak bladder. Do you have that? I bet you do.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: We're basically the same, you and me.

jokes.text: 'God, I gotta stop ending on that boring thing. Clowns!'
jokes.setup: Leslie ends a talking head with a dry list of Harvest Festival statistics.
jokes.punchline: She immediately criticizes herself and tacks on 'Clowns!' as a more exciting ending, self-directing her own confessional.
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-mockumentary gag — Leslie is so performatively enthusiastic that she critiques her own talking head like a producer would and tries to improve it in real time. It's character-specific and adds a self-aware layer to the show's form without breaking it. Good craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We are no longer friends. I don't want to see you. Get out of my office.

jokes.text: 'Man, you are just knocking these off. You're like a ninja crossed with a Jedi, or something. You're like a nerd mixed with a dork or something.'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to compliment Ben's work efficiency with an action-hero comparison.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts the cool compliment with 'You're like a nerd mixed with a dork,' not realizing (or not caring) that he just insulted him.
jokes.explanation: Decent character comedy — Tom's social obliviousness and desire to be cool while accidentally being insulting is on-brand. The structure is a mild setup/undercut. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You want to put a salad cart next to a corn dog stand? That's like putting a diabetic across from a donut shop. It's inhumane. Vegetables are what food eats.

jokes.text: 'Tom, Star Wars is not that nerdy.' / 'No, Star Wars is not that nerdy. It's not, everyone's seen it.'
jokes.setup: Tom implies Star Wars is nerdy as part of his joke.
jokes.punchline: Both Ben and Tom simultaneously protest that Star Wars isn't nerdy — revealing their mutual nerd defensiveness.
jokes.explanation: A light but functional moment — the comedy comes from the unexpected united front between Tom and Ben, both suddenly defensive about their pop culture. Character-consistent but not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, I ended on that? That's so boring. Let me just— Clowns!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know why I said that, but it felt better.

jokes.text: The battle of Indian Hill: 93-year-old Chief Wakote was 'shot 102 times by the cavalry.' Ben asks, 'Did he die?' Ken says, 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Ken describes an epic seven-day battle the Wamapoke lost because 'they didn't have any weapons.' A 93-year-old chief was shot 102 times.
jokes.punchline: Ben's completely sincere, confused question 'Did he die?' followed by Ken's flat, one-word 'Yes.'
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in economy. The setup is already funny (102 shots, no weapons, 93-year-old chief), but the punchline is Ben's completely genuine question — asking the obvious to an absurd degree — followed by Ken's single-word response that makes Ben's question even more ridiculous in retrospect. Every element earns its place. The dark history is handled with the show's characteristic satirical respect. This is a top-tier joke in the episode, scoring 8+ because it's layered, efficient, and the comedic timing of 'Yes.' is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, you're a really smart, talented guy. You're going to do great things.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, you're a really smart, talented guy. You're going to do great things... for someone else's company.

jokes.text: 'And this moment will be commemorated for the next seven days with shooting galleries and fried dough stands.'
jokes.setup: Ken describes the sacred battle site and the tragedy of Chief Wakote's death.
jokes.punchline: He notes with dry sarcasm that this is being 'commemorated' with carnival shooting galleries and fried dough — the contrast between tragedy and celebration is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Ken Hotate is doing sophisticated satirical work here — the irony is genuinely cutting and the specificity (shooting galleries, particularly given the cavalry's role) is excellent. The joke earns its darkness because it's rooted in real cultural critique delivered through character. An 8 because the character integration and structure are both very strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ken Hotate
dialogue.line: How.

jokes.text: Leslie produces a map of 'all the atrocities the Pawnee settlers inflicted upon the Wamapoke Indians' — the atrocities are in blue.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to argue the carnival can still take place despite the site's history.
jokes.punchline: She has already made a detailed, color-coded atrocity map — 'The atrocities are in blue' — as if this is normal municipal preparation.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Leslie-specific: the joke is that she has over-prepared for even the most awkward conversation — she has literally color-coded historical atrocities as background material. 'The atrocities are in blue' is perfectly deadpan. This only makes sense coming from Leslie, who would absolutely make this map. High character integration justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: The Battle of Hastings was one of the bloodiest battles in medieval history. Thousands of soldiers were slaughtered on that field.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wow, that's terrible. Did anyone win?

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: Yes, the Normans won. That's why we're speaking English and not French.

jokes.text: Ken Hotate's talking head: 'There are two things I know about white people. They love Matchbox 20, and they are terrified of curses.'
jokes.setup: Ken has just threatened the festival with the possibility of an ancestral curse.
jokes.punchline: In his talking head, he reveals his dry understanding of white psychology — Matchbox 20 and curse-fear — making clear the curse threat is a strategic tool.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and among the best in the series. It does everything: the structure is perfect (two-part list with a devastating punchline on the second item), the character integration is exceptional (Ken is playing the entire town, using their superstitions as a tool — making him one of the smartest characters in the episode), the Matchbox 20 detail is brilliantly specific and absurd, and it reframes everything we just saw. The joke also has a satirical bite — it acknowledges the colonial power dynamic by showing Ken wielding the one tool available to him. This is a quote that leaves the episode. Justified 9+ score by every metric.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: As you can see from this map, we have color-coded all the major historical atrocities by region and severity. The blue represents minor incidents, yellow for moderate, and red for the really bad stuff. It's actually quite efficient when you organize it this way.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben saying 'Take that, curse!' after getting the cotton candy donation.
jokes.setup: The curse has been threatened. Leslie announces Sweetums donated more cotton candy machines.
jokes.punchline: Both immediately say 'Take that, curse!' — treating cotton candy as a supernatural defense.
jokes.explanation: A light running gag initiation — the comedy is in taking the curse seriously enough to feel like you're winning against it with mundane festival logistics. The synchronized delivery from both characters gives it extra charm.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: I'm terrified of curse words. Like, genuinely afraid of them. So when someone puts on Matchbox 20, I get anxious because I'm always waiting for them to say something bad. But they never do. It's just 'push' and 'smooth' and... nothing. Which somehow makes it worse.

jokes.text: Two characters hit each other in the chest with what sounds like toy weapons or a game — 'Ouch, ouch, ouch! Right in the chest, ooh! Ow, ow, ow! Bazooka!'
jokes.setup: A transition into the carnival setup shows Andy and April playing with something at a game booth.
jokes.punchline: The exaggerated pain sounds followed by 'Bazooka!' and someone off-camera telling them to 'get a room' suggests romantic horseplay being mistaken for something else.
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy that characterizes Andy and April's playful relationship. The 'get a room' reaction is the punchline — suggesting observers read their play-fighting as romantic. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This calls for a celebration! We got the cotton candy machines!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yes! This is amazing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We should do an elaborate pretend combat to celebrate.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? Why would we do that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because we're cursed! We have to fight the curse with our wits and our cotton candy machines!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we're not cursed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not anymore we're not! En garde!

jokes.text: 'Joan is always looking for a scandal. She's like an eagle-eyed tiger.'
jokes.setup: Leslie warns the team about Joan Callamezzo's journalist instincts.
jokes.punchline: The metaphor 'eagle-eyed tiger' is a nonsensical mixed animal hybrid delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: A classic Leslie malaprop/mixed metaphor — she confidently produces a meaningless hybrid image. Works because it's character-specific and delivered without any awareness it's strange.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Joan Callamezzo is the host of Pawnee Today, the local news show. She's been hosting it for like thirty years.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, Joan Callamezzo? That's an amazing band name!

jokes.text: 'Eagle-eyed tiger! New band name, I call it!'
jokes.setup: Leslie uses the phrase 'eagle-eyed tiger.'
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately and enthusiastically stakes his claim to it as a band name — his constant desire to brand everything is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Tom's spontaneous brand-claiming of random phrases is very character-specific and the timing is sharp. The joke is in his complete unselfconsciousness — he has no band but he's already claiming names. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He said he needed space to figure things out, so he broke up with me but then kept texting me about his feelings and asking me to listen to his problems.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, I do that all the time.

jokes.text: 'Let's grab hands.' / 'I don't hold hands.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to do a team huddle and invites everyone to grab hands.
jokes.punchline: Ron flatly refuses — 'I don't hold hands' — as if it's a settled personal policy.
jokes.explanation: Five words that are entirely Ron Swanson. The refusal is absolute, non-negotiable, and absurdly serious. High character integration — this line could only come from Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm handling the breakup really well. I've been going to the gym, eating healthy, and I even started a new hobby.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Day three: I'm eating ice cream straight from the container while watching our favorite show.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Day five: I've rewatched all his Instagram posts. Twice.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Day seven: I'm in his apartment building parking lot. I don't know why I'm here.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Day ten: I've memorized his work schedule. I sit across the street. We make eye contact. I wave. He drives away faster.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'inspiring' speech ends with '...not focus on the fact that if one thing goes wrong, we're all gonna lose our jobs.' Someone responds: 'That's not inspiring.'
jokes.setup: Leslie gives an uplifting pep talk to the team.
jokes.punchline: She accidentally undermines the entire thing by reminding them of catastrophic stakes, and someone immediately calls it out.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's anxiety sabotaging her own pep talk is a classic bit of character comedy — she can't help but include the terrifying caveat. The deadpan 'That's not inspiring' is the perfect button. Good structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The key to a successful relationship is independence. You need to maintain your own interests, your own space, your own identity.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's actually really good advice, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: My mailman said the same thing last week.

jokes.text: Ann's breakup post-mortem: sobbing at a pizza buffet until they asked her to leave, $700 in candles from Anthropologie, looking at dog adoption websites, and 'I did this to my hair.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how Ann is doing after her breakup with Chris.
jokes.punchline: Ann lists an escalating series of breakup behaviors that each become more specific and pathetic, culminating in the undescribed but clearly disastrous hair change.
jokes.explanation: An excellent escalation joke with each item funnier than the last. The pizza buffet eviction is specific and sad in the right way, the $700 Anthropologie candles is brilliant brand-specific detail, and 'I did this to my hair' works as a visual punchline because we can presumably see it. The escalation structure is well-executed and the specificity elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Red leather, yellow leather.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Shaquille O'Neal and Shakira sharp-shoot shrimp.

jokes.text: Leslie's advice to Ann: 'Normally, people tell you to talk about your problems. I'm gonna recommend you bottle that noise up. That's what my mailman said.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is comforting Ann about her breakup.
jokes.punchline: She gives terrible advice — the opposite of standard wisdom — and then cites her mailman as the source.
jokes.explanation: The mailman citation is what elevates this from a standard 'bad advice' joke. It implies Leslie has been getting life guidance from her mailman and finds it authoritative, which is deeply funny. Good economy and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look at this beautiful ferris wheel!

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: That's a wheel of death. One mechanical failure and you're plummeting to your doom.

jokes.text: 'Muah-muah-murder. Murdering the most melons. Shaquille showered shame on Shakira's sheets.'
jokes.setup: A voice is heard warming up or practicing alliteration in the background before Joan's arrival.
jokes.punchline: The escalating alliterative phrases become increasingly bizarre and violent in content.
jokes.explanation: Likely Joan Callamezzo or her crew warming up before the interview — the comedy is in the absurd escalation of alliterative phrases from nonsense to celebrity gossip. 'Shaquille showered shame on Shakira's sheets' is memorably specific. Entertaining background absurdism.

jokes.text: Joan asks if the corn is Pawnee corn or Eagleton corn — with clear distaste for Eagleton.
jokes.setup: Leslie shows off Indiana's largest corn maze.
jokes.punchline: Joan's first question is a loaded civic rivalry question — is this Pawnee or (inferior) Eagleton corn?
jokes.explanation: A quick nod to the Eagleton rivalry that longtime fans appreciate. Not a powerhouse joke but efficiently characterizes Joan and the Pawnee-Eagleton dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I don't see what all the fuss is about. This festival is a waste of time and—

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Is that... Little Sebastian?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: He's beautiful. I was wrong about everything. This is the best day of my life.

jokes.text: Joan: 'But deadly. When was the last time this giant wheel of death was inspected?'
jokes.setup: Leslie proudly shows off the beautiful Ferris wheel.
jokes.punchline: Joan immediately reframes it as a 'giant wheel of death,' looking for the scandal angle in every attraction.
jokes.explanation: Joan's character is perfectly distilled into this moment — she literally cannot see a Ferris wheel without reframing it as an instrument of death. 'Giant wheel of death' is a good phrase. Character integration is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Thank you. I've been working out.

jokes.text: Joan: 'How many of these carnies are illegals?'
jokes.setup: Leslie patiently answers Joan's hostile questions.
jokes.punchline: Joan's next question is instantly offensive and baseless — another attempted scandal with zero evidence.
jokes.explanation: Quick and characterizing — Joan's tabloid-journalist instincts mean she assumes every venue is hiding a scandal. The rapid-fire nature of her hostile questions builds a comedic rhythm. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Joan, you look amazing. Have you lost weight or gained confidence?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Both.

jokes.text: Larry Bird's 84-year-old aunt Tilda signing autographs. 'You got Tilda?' / 'We got Tilda.'
jokes.setup: Leslie lists celebrity appearances at the festival including Larry Bird's 84-year-old aunt.
jokes.punchline: Joan drops her hostile demeanor and is genuinely impressed — 'You got Tilda?' — treating an elderly woman's tenuous celebrity connection as a major booking.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Pawnee-specific joke — the town's standards for celebrity are so low that an 84-year-old woman with a basketball player nephew is a genuine get. Joan's sudden genuine excitement ('You got Tilda?') punctures her hostile journalist persona beautifully. The mirrored 'We got Tilda' confirmation is perfect comedic economy. Scores 8+ because the absurdist specificity (84-year-old aunt specifically, not Larry Bird himself) is excellent writing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Joan, I promise you, this festival is going to blow your mind. We've got live music, food vendors, a petting zoo...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And if you're not satisfied, I will personally take you out for dinner. And drinks. And we can go back to my place and I can show you my vinyl collection. And we can slow dance. And I will massage your feet. And we can do whatever you want... to completion.

jokes.text: Tom to Joan: 'Thank you, Joan. Li'l Sebastian isn't bad either.'
jokes.setup: Joan admires Li'l Sebastian and says 'He is so adorable.'
jokes.punchline: Tom takes it as a compliment directed at himself and graciously extends it to the horse.
jokes.explanation: Pure Tom Haverford. His narcissism is so total that he hears a compliment to a horse as directed at himself and magnanimously includes the horse as a runner-up. The character integration is flawless — only Tom could deliver this line. The economy is exceptional: he does a lot with very few words.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm gonna win you so many teddy bears. I'm talking like, hundreds of teddy bears.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, you can't win hundreds of teddy bears at a carnival.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, fine. Fifty teddy bears.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's still impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Twenty-five teddy bears. Final offer. I'm not going any lower.

jokes.text: Tom to Joan: 'This Harvest Festival, it's gonna knock your socks off. And when it does, I'm gonna be there to give you a foot massage... to completion.' / 'Good lord.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to charm Joan Callamezzo during her walk-through.
jokes.punchline: 'To completion' added to a foot massage offer takes a weird idea and makes it disturbingly suggestive, then Joan's 'Good lord' is the perfect horrified button.
jokes.explanation: Tom's delusional flirtatiousness is well-established and this is a good expression of it. 'To completion' is doing all the work — it transforms a weird offer into an inappropriately suggestive one. Joan's reaction is the right button. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I love you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Awesome sauce!

jokes.text: Ben and Leslie's Teddy bear negotiation: 'I'm gonna win you a million Teddy bears.' / 'Well, I want a billion Teddy bears.' / 'Well, that's a little unrealistic. This is a hard game. Two million.'
jokes.setup: Ben tries to impress Leslie by promising to win her carnival prizes.
jokes.punchline: The negotiation escalates from romantic gesture to absurd economics — Leslie counters with a billion, Ben walks it back to two million as a realistic compromise, treating the impossible as a haggling situation.
jokes.explanation: A delightful escalation joke that also works as character comedy — Ben's auditor brain immediately applies economic logic to a romantic gesture, creating a negotiation where the 'realistic' counteroffer is still impossible. The structure is tight and the humor builds through each exchange. Scores 8 because it's well-constructed and specifically characterizes both Ben's analytical nature and Leslie's whimsy.

jokes.text: Andy yells 'Hey, I love you!' apparently at the carnival, and an off-screen voice yells back 'Dude, shut up!' followed by 'That is awesome sauce!'
jokes.setup: Andy apparently shouts his love declaration during a public carnival game or activity.
jokes.punchline: A stranger tells him to shut up; Andy responds with 'awesome sauce' — which sets up the April plot.
jokes.explanation: Functional moment that's primarily important for plot setup (the 'awesome sauce' vs 'I love you too' issue). The yelled love declaration with a stranger's annoyed reaction is characteristically Andy. Gets a rewatch bonus because it's foreshadowing the episode's emotional B-plot.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: So Ben, tell me about your failures.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I was the mayor of Ice Town when I was 18 years old.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I thought we could create a new winter sports mecca by building an ice rink in a landlocked suburb.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It cost the town $7 million and shut down after only two months.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was also known as Ice Town as a result.

jokes.text: Tom talking-head: 'Most people look at Li'l Sebastian and they see a famous mini horse. I see an advertising opportunity for my club. The Snakehole Lounge.'
jokes.setup: Li'l Sebastian is beloved by all for his own sake.
jokes.punchline: Tom cannot conceive of any situation that isn't a marketing opportunity — he's put Snakehole Lounge branding on a 25-year-old arthritic horse.
jokes.explanation: Tom's relentless brand-brain is perfectly captured here. The irony of treating a beloved public figure as an ad vehicle is well-structured, and character integration is very high.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was a state auditor, I was deputy city manager, I was city manager, I was on the city council, but nobody ever wants to talk about the time I played shortstop for the Sweetwater Wildcats.

jokes.text: 'Wow, that is a shockingly huge mini horse erection.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been describing his Snakehole Lounge branding on Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.punchline: Someone matter-of-factly observes the horse's unexpected physical state — the clinical delivery of a shocking observation.
jokes.explanation: A surprise crude joke delivered completely straight — the comedy is entirely in the deadpan delivery of something shocking. Short, to the point, gets its laugh. The adverb 'shockingly' is doing good work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, Little Sebastian is missing and it's clearly your fault.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, I had nothing to do with it!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh really? Then why are you getting so defensive about it? That's exactly what someone who kidnapped a miniature horse would say.

jokes.text: Joan asks Ben about Ice Town, then he adds unprompted: 'I was also short-stop on my JV baseball team. No one ever brings that up.'
jokes.setup: Joan presses Ben about his past failure bankrupting a city as an 18-year-old mayor.
jokes.punchline: Ben, apparently feeling underappreciated, volunteers that he was also a JV shortstop — as if this balances the ledger — and notes bitterly that no one brings it up.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully observed character comedy. In the middle of a public takedown about a citywide disaster, Ben's wounded pride latches onto his minor athletic achievement as a counterweight — and nobody cares. 'No one ever brings that up' is devastating and perfectly delivered. The joke reveals Ben's character (he needs to be competent; he feels diminished) while being very funny. Scores 8+ because the specificity (JV shortstop, not even varsity) and the resentment embedded in the final line are expertly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Wait, there's a scandal? Oh no. Okay, we need to get ahead of this. Start gathering negative footage immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I want everything. Bad potholes, broken streetlights, spooky traffic lights, anything that makes the city look incompetent.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I was also short-stop on my JV baseball team. No one ever brings that up.'
jokes.setup: Joan lists Ben's failures (Ice Town, bankrupted city); Ben tries to deflect
jokes.punchline: Ben adds his JV baseball position as if it's a mitigating credential — and notes its lack of coverage as a grievance
jokes.explanation: Great Ben Wyatt character comedy. Under pressure, he reaches for a completely irrelevant, minor credential (JV shortstop!) and then complains about its media neglect. The indignation of 'no one ever brings that up' makes it. Very quotable, well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We have a lightning rod problem, a lightning rod staffing issue, and a lightning rod budget shortfall.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, those are just regular problems. A lightning rod is a metal rod that prevents lightning strikes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know what a lightning rod is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, that's a pony, not a mini horse.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Somebody left the gate open and he got out, Jerry!' / 'What are you talking about?' / 'Unbelievable. Another in a long string of miserable failures. You lost Li'l Sebastian!' / 'I wasn't even here!' / 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Li'l Sebastian has escaped. Tom was actually the one who left.
jokes.punchline: Tom blames Jerry, Jerry defends himself by saying he wasn't there, and Tom uses that absence as the very proof of his failure — 'Exactly' — weaponizing Jerry's alibi against him.
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant joke: Jerry's defense ('I wasn't even here!') is turned into the accusation ('Exactly') in one word. Tom's logic is perfectly circular and entirely self-serving, and the reversal is executed flawlessly. The show's running joke of Jerry being blamed for everything reaches a new peak of absurdity here because Tom uses Jerry's innocence as proof of his guilt. Justified 8+ — the single-word reversal is excellent comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Do people really believe in curses?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I don't know, Ben. Let me check with the hundreds of people who've called me about the curse on the old Ramsett house. Or the guy who won't go near the bridge because his grandfather told him it was cursed. Or literally every single person in this town who has a weird superstition. So yes, Ben, people believe in curses.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben say 'Take that, curse!' again, then immediately panic-face when asked what the curse is.
jokes.setup: The press tour went well. Both say 'Take that, curse!' in celebration — then a reporter asks what the curse is.
jokes.punchline: The callback phrase immediately backfires, introducing the curse to the media they were trying to hide it from.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed callback that turns the running gag into a plot complication. The joke works because the phrase they've been gleefully repeating becomes the rope they hang themselves with. Good structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He probably just needed space. Sometimes when you're in a relationship, you feel suffocated and you just need to get away from everything and everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, are you talking about Little Sebastian or about Derek?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm talking about the horse.

jokes.text: Joan: 'Let's get some shots of chipped paint and crying babies. How about some of those spooky traffic lights.'
jokes.setup: Joan immediately pivots to covering the 'curse' narrative
jokes.punchline: Her specific, cynical checklist of B-roll items to manufacture ominous news coverage
jokes.explanation: Excellent media satire. Joan's specific B-roll shopping list ('crying babies,' 'spooky traffic lights') is both a perfect parody of local TV news construction and a great character beat. 'Spooky traffic lights' in particular is funny — they're not inherently spooky, Joan just needs them to be.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Horses love mazes. They're like, super smart. I read that somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's... not true.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, no, I'm pretty sure horses love mazes. They'll definitely find Little Sebastian.

jokes.text: Leslie explains the triple/quadruple lightning rod situation: 'Plus we lost that little pony.' / 'It's a mini horse!' as an aside amid crisis.
jokes.setup: Ben is cataloging the compounding crises facing the festival.
jokes.punchline: Someone interrupts his dire crisis analysis to correct the pony/mini horse distinction — the same correction from the beginning of the episode, now even more absurd amid genuine catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed callback to the pony/mini horse distinction that's funnier in context because someone is pedantically correcting semantics during a multi-front crisis. The comedy of misplaced priorities is very Parks and Rec.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are such a powerful, strong woman. And your skin is absolutely glowing right now.

jokes.text: Ben's analysis: 'This is a huge government project, already a lightning rod. Wamapoke controversy — double lightning rod. Lost the little pony — triple lightning rod. The curse — quadruple lightning rod.'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to explain how bad the situation is.
jokes.punchline: His management-consultant brain turns a cascading disaster into a tidy numbered metaphor — 'quadruple lightning rod' — as if naming it properly is solving it.
jokes.explanation: Ben's systematic audit-brain turning chaos into a numbered framework is character-specific and the escalating lightning rod metaphor is funny. The joke is that naming it 'quadruple' doesn't help at all.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that me? Did they just show my butt?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: That's not what happened at all!

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: But... that was pretty cool.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Wait, I'm sorry. Do people in this town really believe in curses?' / Leslie: 'Oh, no. No. We all just behave rationally and believe we are all in charge of our own destinies. Come on.'
jokes.setup: Ben expresses genuine shock that the curse is being taken seriously.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response is completely sincere reassurance that Pawnee is rational — delivered in a tone that makes absolutely clear the opposite is true.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's completely unironic defense of Pawnee's rationality — in the middle of a curse panic — is perfect. She genuinely believes this, which makes it funnier. Strong character integration and irony.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so corn and maize are the same thing?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Then why do they have different names? I thought maize was, like, a ancient Aztec word for corn.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It is.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So if maize is the Aztec word, then corn must be the... I dunno, the British word for it? Like how they call elevators 'lifts'?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No. Corn is just... corn.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, I'm pretty sure 'corn' comes from a kernel. Like, a corn kernel? So they named the whole thing after the kernel?

jokes.text: Tom suggests Li'l Sebastian escaped because 'he tried to share his true feelings with someone and they didn't reciprocate.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks how Li'l Sebastian could have gotten out.
jokes.punchline: Tom projects his own romantic drama onto the horse with complete seriousness.
jokes.explanation: Tom attributing his own romantic anxieties to a horse is absurdist and character-specific. Also retroactively positions Tom as someone nursing his own emotional issues, giving a layer to his behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey, what's wrong? Talk to me.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm leaving. I'm going to Venezuela and I'm never coming back.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Venezuela? April, come on—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've made up my mind. It's final.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Good idea. Horses love mazes, come on!'
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Andy and April to check the corn maze for Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.punchline: Andy enthusiastically endorses this as a good idea based on the (completely made-up) premise that horses love mazes.
jokes.explanation: Pure Andy — confidently asserts false animal behavior facts with complete conviction. Short, character-specific, and funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Bodybuilder
dialogue.line: Hey beautiful, you must be a magnet because I'm attracted to you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's actually concerning. Magnetic fields can interfere with medical devices like pacemakers.

dialogue.speaker: Bodybuilder
dialogue.line: No, I just meant... never mind. My shoulders are killing me anyway.

jokes.text: 'Ah, good. Anne, you're so beautiful. Beautiful Anne.' — Leslie randomly and sincerely complimenting Ann in the middle of a crisis.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in full crisis mode giving rapid instructions to Ann.
jokes.punchline: She pauses to sincerely, warmly, and randomly compliment Ann on her appearance — completely unprompted — before continuing her crisis management.
jokes.explanation: One of the most Leslie moments in the episode — her deep genuine affection for Ann breaks through even in crisis mode. The joke works because it's completely sincere (not sarcastic), completely random in context, and deeply characterizing. Only Leslie Knope interrupts disaster management to tell her best friend she's beautiful. High character integration justifies 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He's not boyfriend material.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Girl, you don't need a boyfriend. You need a man who can do things. This guy can move furniture, he can intimidate people at the bank, he can open jars. Use him.

jokes.text: 'Okay, run, Anne, run!' — Leslie's final instruction to Ann.
jokes.setup: Leslie gives Ann detailed instructions about treating and releasing a patient without media contact.
jokes.punchline: She ends the instructions with 'Run, Anne, run!' — as though Anne needs to literally sprint from the situation.
jokes.explanation: A small, charming bit — Leslie's urgency escalating to the point of telling Ann to literally run. Shows her panic bleeding into her communication style.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Did you guys find Little Sebastian?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, Jerry, we didn't find a tiny horse. What do you think we've been doing all day?

jokes.text: News broadcast shows 'exclusive animation' of Leslie refusing to move the carnival — depicted as a cartoon Leslie violently shoving Ken Hotate.
jokes.setup: A news anchor says they have exclusive animation of the conversation between Leslie and Ken.
jokes.punchline: The animation clearly depicts something that never happened — Leslie shoving Ken — and the anchor treats it as factual documentary footage.
jokes.explanation: A sharp media satire joke — the animation convention (used by real news to depict events they have no footage of) is taken to its logical absurd extreme. The animation apparently shows something completely fabricated, presented as news. The anchor's excited 'I love these things' is the button. Scores 8+ because it's a well-observed media satire that's both character-funny (Leslie's horror) and structurally strong.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I need to address some rumors that are going around. No, I did not have an affair with the city manager. No, I am not running an illegal gambling ring out of my office. And absolutely not, I am not feasting on petting zoo animals.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know where that last one came from, but it needs to stop.

jokes.text: The anchor says 'I love these things. Sorry.' after watching his own channel's deceptive animation.
jokes.setup: The news animation depicting false events plays on air.
jokes.punchline: The anchor momentarily breaks from reporter mode to express personal delight at the animation, then half-heartedly apologizes.
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley's cheerful obliviousness is perfectly captured — he's delighted by the animated segment even as it slanders someone, and the 'sorry' is perfunctory at best. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So you're saying this could be a disaster?

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: On a scale of one to ten, I'd say it's somewhere between a disaster and a catastrophe.

jokes.text: Andy to April in the corn maze: 'You know how Indians call corn maize? This is why. I never knew that.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are searching for Li'l Sebastian in the corn maze.
jokes.punchline: Andy has an 'aha' moment about the etymology of the word 'maize,' experiencing a genuine revelation about something obvious — and has clearly never made this connection before.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Andy joke — his childlike wonder at an obvious linguistic connection he's just discovered is pure character. The addition of 'I never knew that' makes it clear he's genuinely moved by this minor insight. Scores 8+ because the character integration is exceptional and the joke is very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Perd Hapley
dialogue.line: Yes, I have a question, and here it is: do you have any comment on the comment that was made about the comment?

jokes.text: April says she might be going to Venezuela. 'Tomorrow. Forever.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks if April is okay because she seems upset.
jokes.punchline: April mentions possibly moving to Venezuela forever as a casual aside — the extreme solution delivered completely flat.
jokes.explanation: Classic April deadpan — the extreme emotional response (emigrating to South America permanently) delivered as an afterthought. The two-word follow-up 'Forever.' is perfectly calibrated. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Son of a biscuit!

jokes.text: April says: 'I'm not mad at Andy. Andy's great. I awesome sauce Andy.'
jokes.setup: Andy tries to figure out why April is upset with him. April denies being upset and says she loves him using his own stupid phrase.
jokes.punchline: April using 'awesome sauce' as a verb meaning love — directly mirroring the phrase that caused the problem and revealing her feelings through it.
jokes.explanation: April adopting Andy's dumb slang to express her love is both a perfect callback and a character moment — she won't say 'I love you' in the conventional way, so she weaponizes his own verbal tic. It's sweet and funny simultaneously. High character integration and earned emotional payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Crowd
dialogue.line: It's Jerry's fault!

dialogue.speaker: Crowd
dialogue.line: Yeah, Jerry did this!

dialogue.speaker: Crowd
dialogue.line: Blame Jerry!

jokes.text: Ann to Donna: 'He isn't exactly boyfriend material.' Donna: 'Who said anything about a boyfriend? Use him, abuse him, lose him.'
jokes.setup: Ann is watching Donna flirt with a patient and offers a judgment
jokes.punchline: Donna delivers her relationship philosophy in three perfectly parallel, rhyming verbs
jokes.explanation: Donna's three-verb philosophy is a quotable, perfectly structured line. The rhyme scheme (use/abuse/lose) gives it a memorable rhythm, and the escalation from 'use' to 'abuse' to 'lose' is both funny and completely character-consistent. Donna's confidence in delivering it as obvious wisdom makes it land harder. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He's been missing for three weeks. He's dead.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron! Ron, don't say that. We don't know that for sure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, a small horse doesn't just disappear. He's dead.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You don't know that! He could be in Canada!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He's dead.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Yeah, Jerry. He's right here in my pocket.' — Tom's sarcastic response to Jerry asking if they found Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.setup: Jerry hopefully asks if they've found the horse.
jokes.punchline: Tom's sarcastic 'He's right here in my pocket' — making clear what a stupid question it was.
jokes.explanation: Standard sarcasm with decent character integration (Tom's contempt for Jerry). Not exceptional but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Everyone stop. I have a solution. Leslie, you're in charge of the parks department. Tom, you're fired. April, you're doing Leslie's old job. Jerry, you're still Jerry. Andy, I don't know what you do, so I'm firing you too. Meeting adjourned.

jokes.text: Tom's solution to the ground search failing: 'We need a bird's eye view.' / Immediately cuts to Ron apparently being asked to climb the Ferris wheel.
jokes.setup: Tom announces they need a bird's eye view to spot Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.punchline: The solution is apparently to have Ron climb the Ferris wheel — Ron's impassive face processing this request is the implied visual joke.
jokes.explanation: The implicit joke of Ron being chosen for Ferris wheel reconnaissance is funny — Ron's stoic competence being applied to absurd tasks is classic. The cut is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I know I messed up with the whole 'awesome sauce' thing.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, you did.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I was thinking... maybe we could make it awesome sauce again? Together?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is that a yes?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's a yes.

jokes.text: Leslie's press conference: denying there is 'no food shortage' and that Parks staff were NOT 'feasting on petting zoo animals.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to address false rumors about the festival.
jokes.punchline: She has to formally deny that her staff ate the petting zoo animals — a rumor so specific and horrible that the denial itself is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The 'feasting on petting zoo animals' denial is one of the episode's best absurdist jokes. The very specificity of the rumor (not just eating animals — feasting, specifically petting zoo animals) combined with Leslie needing to formally state this didn't happen is perfectly calibrated. It suggests the media environment has gotten so chaotic that this specific thing became a story. Scores 8 for strong structure, originality, and the fact that the denial format itself is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I didn't do it!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Jerry, everyone heard it.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It was my chair! My chair makes that noise when I sit down. It's an old chair.

jokes.text: Joan: 'You were in charge of watching a tiny horse, and you failed.' Tom: 'Look, I'm only gonna say this once. What if Li'l Sebastian is on this Ferris wheel?' / 'How about you only say that never.'
jokes.setup: Tom is being called out publicly for losing Li'l Sebastian.
jokes.punchline: Tom's defensive pivot — floating the completely nonsensical theory that Li'l Sebastian is ON the Ferris wheel — and Ben shutting it down with perfect economy.
jokes.explanation: Tom's absurd deflection paired with Ben's perfect shutdown. 'How about you only say that never' is excellent line structure — the mirrored format ('only say this once' / 'only say that never') is well-crafted. Tom's attempt to redirect suspicion to the Ferris wheel is hilariously desperate. Justifies 8+ for structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wow, Ed, you really know your stuff about generators. That's impressive.

dialogue.speaker: Ed
dialogue.line: Thanks, Leslie. Hey, since we're both here and everything's kind of crazy right now... would you maybe want to grab dinner sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ed, there's a town-wide power outage happening.

dialogue.speaker: Ed
dialogue.line: I know, but I figured now's as good a time as any to shoot my shot.

jokes.text: Joan: 'How big of a disaster will this be, on a scale of 9 to 10?'
jokes.setup: A reporter asks Leslie how big of a disaster the festival will be.
jokes.punchline: The scale given — 9 to 10 — presupposes disaster is inevitable and the only question is severity.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant little journalism satire joke — the 'scale of 9 to 10' is a perfectly constructed trap question that normalizes disaster as a certainty. It's highly quotable, efficiently structured, and precisely characterizes the adversarial local media. Scores 8+ because the joke is original in its construction and the economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I'm not above begging. In fact, historically, some of the greatest leaders have had to beg. Joan of Arc begged the French army to fight. Gandhi begged the British to leave India.

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: And they were both killed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, well, different times.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley's question: 'Yeah, the statement that this reporter has is a question.'
jokes.setup: Leslie opens the press conference for questions.
jokes.punchline: Perd announces his question by first declaring it to be a question — a completely redundant statement that is apparently his verbal tic.
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley's defining verbal tic — redundantly prefacing his questions by announcing they are questions — is brilliantly character-specific and a recurring source of comedy throughout the series. 'The statement that this reporter has is a question' is perfectly circular logic delivered with complete gravitas. The character integration score is as high as it gets. Scores 8+ because the joke is endlessly quotable, deeply character-specific, and was clearly a carefully crafted verbal construction.

dialogue.speaker: Bodybuilder
dialogue.line: You need to leave so I can make out with Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: *salutes mockingly*

jokes.text: The power goes out in the middle of Leslie's press conference — lights die and the tent collapses or goes dark.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in the middle of confidently telling everyone there is no curse.
jokes.punchline: The power immediately goes out — perfect comic timing making it seem like divine/curse-level retribution for her denial.
jokes.explanation: Structurally perfect: Leslie says 'you know as well as I do there's no such [thing as a curse]' and the universe immediately contradicts her. The timing is the joke — it's a classic sitcom structure elevated by its specific context (a press conference denial of a supernatural claim). The structure score is very high because the setup and payoff are elegantly arranged.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ken, can you help me with the generator?

dialogue.speaker: Ken
dialogue.line: Sure, I'd be happy to help. Just like the government was happy to help the Native Americans.

jokes.text: 'Crap on a spatula. It's the curse. That's exactly what it is.'
jokes.setup: The power goes out during Leslie's denial of the curse.
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately and definitively attributes it to the curse — with a colorful expletive substitute.
jokes.explanation: 'Crap on a spatula' is a fun Pawnee-appropriate expletive substitute. The immediate pivot to curse acceptance is funny given Leslie just denied it. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So we found Little Sebastian in the corn maze. He got out in like ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry's still in there. We left a trail of breadcrumbs, but he ate those.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Look, you were totally fine until I got involved. So I feel like I should probably just go... I'm the curse, I think.'
jokes.setup: Multiple things have gone wrong since Ben became involved with the festival.
jokes.punchline: Ben internalizes the curse narrative — sincerely believing he might be the supernatural cause — and announces he's removing himself as if that's a logical solution.
jokes.explanation: Ben — the rational auditor who dismissed the curse — has now fully succumbed to the superstition and declared himself the curse. The character arc of a skeptic becoming a believer is compressed into a single absurd moment. Good character integration — it also plays on Ben's Ice Town guilt.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We should probably find Jerry.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But first, I'm going to get a waffle.

jokes.text: Ron's horse timeline assessment: 'If they're missing this long, they're usually dead.' / 'Well, if that's true, then you're gonna have to answer to the whole town. And God.'
jokes.setup: Ron is being consulted on whether Li'l Sebastian can be found alive.
jokes.punchline: Ron's blunt 'usually dead' is so matter-of-fact it shocks; the response escalating to 'the whole town. And God.' escalates the stakes to absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan mortality assessment followed by the invoking of divine judgment (because God presumably cares about Li'l Sebastian) is good absurdist escalation. Character integration strong for Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, Ice Town was a disaster. It cost the city millions of dollars and it was a complete failure.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You were literally memed into oblivion. There are still 'Ice Town Costs Ice Clown' signs up around the city.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I really don't need—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to be mean, I'm just being honest. It was bad. Really bad.

jokes.text: Ron's intervention: 'All of you, be quiet! Andy, she's mad because you said 'awesome sauce' instead of 'I love you, too.' April, he loves you. Stop being a child. Tom, you're clearly at fault. Blaming Jerry won't save you. Jerry, we both know you were shotgunning funnel cakes instead of watching Li'l Sebastian. So everyone apologize to everyone else!'
jokes.setup: Multiple arguments are happening simultaneously in the group
jokes.punchline: Ron, who hates emotional engagement, delivers a perfectly accurate, utterly no-nonsense verdict on all four parties simultaneously — including the damning detail of Jerry shotgunning funnel cakes
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron Swanson's defining character trait is his discomfort with emotions paired with his absolute competence — so him issuing a four-party verdict with complete accuracy, including the devastating 'shotgunning funnel cakes,' is perfect. The Jerry detail is the standout: Ron knows exactly what happened, in vivid detail, and it's both damning and absurdly specific. The structure (four verdicts, one command) is crisp. Highly character-integrated — only Ron would both hate this situation and resolve it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, did you guys hear that? Was that... was that a whinny?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? No, Ben, Little Sebastian's not even here.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Right, right. I know. I just... I thought I heard something majestic.

jokes.text: Andy to April: 'That's what makes the sauce so awesome.'
jokes.setup: Andy tells April he loves her (sincerely, this time) after Ron's intervention.
jokes.punchline: Andy redeems 'awesome sauce' by framing April's love as the literal ingredient that makes it awesome.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful callback resolution — Andy takes the dumb phrase that caused the fight and gives it genuine meaning. 'That's what makes the sauce so awesome' is simultaneously stupid and sincere in the best Parks and Rec way. The earned_vs_cheap score is high because this moment genuinely earns its warmth through the episode's comic setup. The character integration is perfect for Andy.

jokes.text: 'Aw, Jerry just farted!' / 'I'm very upset, I get nervous.'
jokes.setup: The group has just had an emotional resolution moment — apologies, declarations of love.
jokes.punchline: Jerry farts, destroying the tender atmosphere; his explanation ('I get nervous') is somehow worse than the fart.
jokes.explanation: A classic Parks and Rec Jerry moment — he deflates a warm scene. The fart is cheap but the excuse ('I get nervous') is more character-specific. The timing, right after the sweet resolution, is the real craft. Functional lowbrow comedy.

jokes.text: Ed the generator man: 'Wow, you know your stuff. You single?' — flirting with Leslie about generators.
jokes.setup: Leslie demonstrates detailed knowledge of generator specifications in a crisis.
jokes.punchline: Ed is inexplicably attracted to this and immediately asks if she's single — the crisis context makes the flirtation absurdly misplaced.
jokes.explanation: A quick cringe joke — a man hitting on Leslie because of her generator knowledge during a power crisis. Establishes Ed's character and gets a mild laugh. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Ken Hotate: 'Much like the early settlers of Pawnee begged the Wamapoke 200 years ago.' / 'Ah, but that was...' / 'A trick. And over 50 Wamapoke were slaughtered.'
jokes.setup: Leslie comes to Ken on her knees begging for help with the generator.
jokes.punchline: Ken draws a parallel to historical settler begging, Leslie starts to differentiate her situation — and Ken finishes her sentence with 'A trick,' then delivers the casualty count.
jokes.explanation: Ken Hotate's best scene. The joke works because he completes Leslie's sentence in the worst possible way — she was going to say 'different' and he says 'A trick, and 50 people died.' The structure of letting Leslie walk into the historical parallel herself is excellent. Ken's deadpan delivery of historical atrocities as conversational anecdotes is one of the show's best recurring comedic strategies. Scores 8+ for structure, character integration, and dark wit.

jokes.text: The carnival nurse scene — sick man says 'I don't know what's sicker, me or your body.' Nurse rejects him: 'Your loss.'
jokes.setup: A man comes to the first aid tent, presumably as part of the 'curse' illness narrative.
jokes.punchline: He tries to flirt with the nurse using his illness as a pickup line; she shoots him down without hesitation; he remains confident.
jokes.explanation: A quick cringe comedy bit — the delusional confidence of a sick man hitting on a nurse is mildly funny. 'Your loss' from the nurse is a clean button. Functional but not memorable.

jokes.text: Donna says 'Beat it, Donna' to herself and leaves the sick man's tent after he asks her to make out until the lights come back on — then 'Aye, aye, captain.'
jokes.setup: The sick man asks Donna to make out with him until the lights come back on.
jokes.punchline: She declines ('Beat it, Donna') and then immediately changes course ('Aye, aye, captain') — suggesting she changes her mind and goes back.
jokes.explanation: Donna's self-command followed by immediate reversal is perfectly character-specific — she refuses herself and then decides to go anyway. 'Aye, aye, captain' is a great button. The comedy is in her self-directed inner conflict playing out loud.

jokes.text: Ken Hotate: 'A native American tribe making a deal with the government. Heh! What could go wrong?'
jokes.setup: Ken is about to agree to let Leslie use his generator in exchange for a better exhibit placement.
jokes.punchline: Ken himself jokes about the historically terrible track record of such agreements — with a small, knowing laugh before delivering the punch.
jokes.explanation: One of the two or three best jokes in the episode. Ken Hotate using ironic understatement about the entire history of broken treaties between the U.S. government and Native American tribes — delivered in a single sardonic sentence — is exceptional. The 'Heh!' before it is perfectly placed, making clear he knows exactly what he's doing. The economy is near-perfect: the entire weight of centuries of history is compressed into six words. The character integration is flawless. This joke earns a 9+ on craft because it does sophisticated satirical work with complete efficiency and Ken's voice is irreplaceable. It's also highly quotable.

jokes.text: After the ceremony, the news anchor announces Li'l Sebastian is back and 'he gave us a scare' — then cuts to the horse having been found in the corn maze center. 'It took us four hours to solve that maze. It took the horse 15 minutes.'
jokes.setup: The search for Li'l Sebastian is concluded — he was in the corn maze.
jokes.punchline: The humans took four hours to navigate the maze. The arthritic 25-year-old horse with cataracts solved it in 15 minutes.
jokes.explanation: A perfect deflating callback to the corn maze — the supposedly hapless animal humiliated the entire search team. 'Andy says horses love mazes' gets a retroactive payoff. The deadpan delivery of this revelation and the specific '15 minutes' vs. '4 hours' contrast is well-crafted.

jokes.text: News report: 'We spotted him from the top of the ferris wheel at the center of the corn maze. After the power came back on, we went and got him. It took us four hours to solve that maze. It took the horse 15 minutes.'
jokes.setup: They explain how Li'l Sebastian was found in the corn maze
jokes.punchline: The humans took four hours to navigate a maze the horse solved in 15 minutes
jokes.explanation: Clean, effective joke. The inversion — the animal is smarter at navigating the corn maze than the people — is a satisfying beat, and the specific times (four hours vs. 15 minutes) make it concrete and funnier. Li'l Sebastian continues to outclass the humans.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I suppose I oughta go look for him. Right after I get a bratwurst.' — about Jerry still lost in the corn maze.
jokes.setup: It's revealed Jerry is still lost in the corn maze hours after Li'l Sebastian was found.
jokes.punchline: Ron acknowledges he should look for Jerry but decides to get a bratwurst first — revealing that Jerry's welfare is comfortably below a sausage in Ron's priority ranking.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson joke. The deadpan prioritization of bratwurst over a colleague's safety is pure character, and 'I suppose I oughta go look for him' already sets up the comic expectation of reluctant responsibility — which the bratwurst pivot then subverts. The economy is exceptional. Among the most quotable lines in the episode. Scores 8.5+ because character integration and economy are both near-perfect.

jokes.text: 'Jerry's still out there.'
jokes.setup: The Li'l Sebastian crisis is resolved and the festival is saved.
jokes.punchline: An afterthought mention that Jerry is still lost in the maze — he's been there hours, nobody has noticed.
jokes.explanation: Four words that land beautifully as the button to the whole Li'l Sebastian search. The comedy is in what's NOT said — no urgency, no plan, just a casual acknowledgment that Jerry has been abandoned in a corn maze during a major festival. The economy score is perfect. It's the funniest Jerry dismissal in the episode precisely because it's so brief and so unconcerned.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Ben: 'Ice Town was a disaster. And it seems like it was probably your fault. From what I can tell, you mismanaged the hell out of it.'
jokes.setup: Ben apologizes for leaving and cites Ice Town as evidence he's jinxed.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, while trying to be supportive, can't help but state the obvious — it was probably his fault — and does so with clinical directness before pivoting to encouragement.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's inability to give pure encouragement without first stating the accurate, unflattering truth is deeply character-specific. 'You mismanaged the hell out of it' delivered as if it's supportive is exactly how Leslie would see this. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: A Wamapoke representative finds Ben after the ceremony and wipes his dirty face, saying 'Oh gosh, you're filthy. Go clean yourself up. Try to look professional.'
jokes.setup: Someone approaches Ben post-ceremony to confirm 'this is the guy' — presumably he was involved in the ceremonial fire or cursed ground.
jokes.punchline: Rather than anything ceremonially significant, the representative simply scolds him for being dirty and tells him to look professional — maternal nagging from an unexpected source.
jokes.explanation: A quick subversion of ceremonial expectation — instead of something mystical, it's just 'clean yourself up.' Gets a mild laugh from the bathetic contrast.

jokes.text: Ben at the end: 'I don't get it. At all. It's kind of a small horse. I mean, what am I missing? Am I crazy?' / 'Hey, Ben, you just missed it. He whinnied.' / 'Oh, yeah, no. I totally heard that. It was great.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is cooing over Li'l Sebastian at the festival's conclusion.
jokes.punchline: Ben finally admits in his talking head he still doesn't get it — then immediately lies to Leslie's face that he heard the whinny and it was great.
jokes.explanation: The perfect closing callback — Ben's episode-long confusion about Li'l Sebastian gets its final resolution: he still doesn't get it, but he'll pretend he does. The talking head honesty immediately followed by the sincere lie to Leslie is structurally excellent. 'Oh, yeah, no. I totally heard that. It was great.' is a masterclass in how to fake enthusiasm. The earned_vs_cheap score is high because this moment has been built across the entire episode. Closes the central comic premise perfectly.

tmdb_overview: It's make it or break it for the Parks Department at the Harvest Festival which is full of surprises.
insight: Event logistics comedy sustains 61 jokes despite middling 72.7 score, outpaced by darker ensemble work.
